Topics:

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alec Park: Okay folks, thanks for joining. We'll kick off, quick intro round then jump into the on-prem specifics that Shoreline flagged in the questionnaire. Maya and Jonah from my side will take the technical parts.
[00:00:18] Ravi Patel: Hi all, thanks. We wanted to focus on how we can run Redwood in our air-walled environment — delivery of artifacts, how licensing works when there's no internet, and how to avoid cold-start latency for KV-heavy chat workloads.
[00:00:35] Maya Chen: Great. We'll start with the artifact story — two main options: pre-signed bundle that you transfer via secure media, or we provide a shipping manifest and script you run to pull from an internal repo. For air-gapped you usually want a signed tarball plus a checksum and our offline license key.
[00:00:52] Marco Vega: When you say signed, is that actually vendor-signed binary signatures we can verify with our HSM?
[00:01:05] Jonah Ruiz: Right, the bundle includes an SHA256 and an RSA signature. We can provide public keys for verification. If you require HSM-signed artifacts we can coordinate with our security team to support an additional signing step — that's usually a separate contract but doable.
[00:01:22] Priya Singh: Do you embed the license in the bundle? We need a separation: license activation should be a separate step so we can audit it and store keys in our HSM.
[00:01:36] Alec Park: Agreed. Our offline licensing flow is separate: we ship the runtime tarball; you run the installer which emits an activation request blob. You send that blob to our licensing endpoint via a security channel (we'll support manual transfer) and we return an activation token that you paste back in. For fully air-gapped we'll accept an emailed blob or secure transfer handled by your security team.
[00:01:58] Dana Lopez: That activation step — does it require outbound connectivity from the target node? We cannot allow outbound in our production cluster.
[00:02:12] Maya Chen: No outbound required. Installer can produce the CSR-like blob. We will manually process it and return a signed token. For audits we log the CSR id and activation id.
[00:02:25] Ravi Patel: Ok good. Next — GPU drivers. We run mixed hardware: A100, H200 and some older V100s. Driver compatibility has been a pain. How picky is your runtime?
[00:02:40] Jonah Ruiz: We support CUDA 11.8 onward and ROCm X.Y for AMD — we maintain a compatibility matrix. For quantized kernels we've got fallback kernels when preferred CUDA kernels aren't available, but perf drops. Important: certain optimizations (like fused attention kernels and NVCOMP compression) require specific driver+cuda combinations.
[00:03:02] Dana Lopez: For H200s do you require signed drivers / vendor modules? We have an enforced driver whitelist.
[00:03:14] Maya Chen: H200 is fine but we need the right NGC / driver stack — we'll provide a tested driver list. If you require vendor-signed modules we can produce an artifact list that contains driver package names and checksums.
[00:03:28] Marco Vega: What about container runtimes — we use CRI-O, Podman on our air-gapped nodes. Any issues?
[00:03:39] Jonah Ruiz: Runtime works with OCI images; we ship both container images and an unpacked filesystem tarball for environments that prefer not to run container engines. For CRI-O should be fine; we just need the right kernel modules loaded for GPUs.
[00:03:55] Priya Singh: On the KV cache — our chat stack has a lot of long-context sessions where KV cache warming dominates first-request latency. Any recommended approach?
[00:04:10] Maya Chen: Two patterns: active prefetch and lazy prefetch. Active prefetch runs a background warmup that primes KV entries for models you expect; lazy prefetch warms per-session on first request but tries to overlap with token generation. For your SLOs — you mentioned 100ms p50, 250ms p95 for single-turn — active prefetch plus an LRU persistent cache works best.
[00:04:33] Ravi Patel: Our p95 is currently 700ms with cold KV — so need to shave that. Can Redwood persist the KV cache across restarts in on-prem?
[00:04:46] Maya Chen: Yes, we support persisted KV snapshots to disk encrypted at rest. For air-gapped we recommend persistent snapshots stored on the node and periodic bundle transfers for snapshot backups. We also support a startup warmup script that streams prior session keys into the runtime.
[00:05:05] Dana Lopez: How large are those snapshots? Some of our nodes have limited local disk.
[00:05:16] Jonah Ruiz: Depends on active sessions and sequence lengths. Typical snapshot for a 2k-session footprint with 4K context might be 200–800MB compressed. If you have hundreds of concurrent sessions, you partition snapshots across pods. We can provide tooling to sample and estimate size based on your logs.
[00:05:35] Ravi Patel: What about batching? We have spikes of bursts with mixed latency-sensitive interactions. We fear batching will blow p95.
[00:05:49] Maya Chen: Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with priority lanes: low-latency requests go to a shallow lane with small batch sizes while throughput requests accumulate in deeper lanes. You can configure target latency SLOs per route or per API key. Mixed-mode batching reduces token cost without sacrificing strict low-SLO traffic.
[00:06:08] Marco Vega: Is that configured via model config? How do we encode the per-route SLOs?
[00:06:18] Jonah Ruiz: It's in the route config: max_batch_ms, batch_size_policy (adaptive or fixed), and lane_priority. We'll share a sample YAML.
[00:06:29] Priya Singh: Quantization — we want int4 for cost reasons but worry about hallucination and quality regressions. What's your guidance?
[00:06:41] Maya Chen: We recommend a staged rollout: run evals on a held-out prompt set with int8 then int4. In our benchmarks int8 retains >98% fidelity in most tasks; int4 can be model dependent. Also pair quantization with a small floating fallback for critical routes. Redwood Optimize can auto-suggest quantization profiles for your workload.
[00:07:05] Ravi Patel: Can the runtime do mixed-precision per-layer?
[00:07:11] Jonah Ruiz: Yes — we support hybrid quantization: critical attention layers in fp16 and weights quantized elsewhere. That lets you preserve quality while cutting memory.
[00:07:21] Marco Vega: For air-gapped environments, how do we get the quantized kernels? Are those included in the signed bundle?
[00:07:30] Maya Chen: Bundles include the kernels compiled for common instruction sets. For specialized kernels (e.g., H200 MIG-like shapes) we include optional kernel packs. If you need to compile on-prem we can provide a build script but that requires toolchain access; for fully offline we supply prebuilt kernel packs.
[00:07:48] Ravi Patel: Bootstrapping: what's the recommended first-run sequence so we minimize warmup pain when we flip traffic?
[00:07:58] Maya Chen: Steps: 1) Install runtime and drivers; verify kernels; 2) Restore last KV snapshot; 3) Run warmup script to prefetch hot prefixes and prime KV; 4) Start in canary with throttled traffic and enable the low-latency lane for critical endpoints; 5) Monitor trace metrics and adjust batch windows. We'll provide a runbook.
[00:08:25] Dana Lopez: For the warmup script — can it run as a Kubernetes Job that reads historical session logs and generates warmup calls?
[00:08:35] Jonah Ruiz: Definitely. Many customers run a periodic job that replays hashed prefixes into the runtime's warmup API. We provide a replay client and examples.
[00:08:47] Priya Singh: About logging/audits in air-gapped: we need to capture activation events and runtime errors but cannot ship logs offsite. Can Redwood's console run in a private control plane?
[00:08:59] Alec Park: Redwood Private provides a customer-managed control plane you run inside your VPC, and for fully offline we support a read-only artifact that contains dashboards you run on-prem. Audit logs can be stored locally and exported per your retention policy.
[00:09:13] Ravi Patel: Any common gotchas you've seen with operator teams doing this first time?
[00:09:20] Maya Chen: A few: driver mismatches, missing kernel modules, insufficient ephemeral storage for KV snapshots, and forgetting to enable hugepages for some kernels. Also, not whitelisting the runtime user for GPU access is a frequent one.
[00:09:36] Marco Vega: About hugepages — we run stock kubelet, not tuned for HPC. Is that a blocker?
[00:09:46] Jonah Ruiz: You don't strictly need hugepages but enabling them improves perf for large contexts. We can run with defaults but expect higher variance in p95. We'll document the kernel tweaks.
[00:09:58] Ravi Patel: Can we run a short benchmark you provide on our fleet without installing full production?
[00:10:06] Maya Chen: Yes — we have a lightweight offline perf harness that runs a canned prompt mix and an optional KV warmup. It outputs p50/p95 token latency, throughput, and memory. We'll include both a container and a tarball.
[00:10:20] Priya Singh: Security question: the activation token — is it long-lived? How do we revoke if a node is decommissioned?
[00:10:29] Alec Park: Activation tokens are tied to host fingerprints and can be revoked from our license portal. For air-gapped we produce a list of active activations you can cross-check; we also support time-limited tokens.
[00:10:42] Dana Lopez: For model updates — how do we handle signed model rollouts offline?
[00:10:50] Jonah Ruiz: We support a model bundle manifest; you stage new model bundles in your internal artifact store and run an offline rollout tool which verifies signatures locally. Rollouts can be canaried across nodes.
[00:10:59] Marco Vega: If we want to keep some routes on int8 and others on fp16, is that a per-route config?
[00:11:07] Maya Chen: Yes, policy is route-level: you can pin model variant and quantization profile per route. That lets you keep mission-critical routes in high-precision while moving background jobs to quantized variants.
[00:11:22] Ravi Patel: Anything about license counts and offline metrics? We price on reserved tokens, right?
[00:11:28] Alec Park: For Private/offline there's a platform licensing model plus optional reserved token commitments if you want predictable economics. We can do a usage meter that writes to a local ledger and you report periodically for billing reconciliation.
[00:11:41] Priya Singh: For compliance, we need full audit logs of who activated what and when. Does your offline portal provide that?
[00:11:49] Jonah Ruiz: Yes — audit logs are part of the private control plane. For fully air-gapped we provide an audit export you ingest into your SIEM.
[00:11:59] Dana Lopez: On the subject of kernel packs — are you shipping pre-compiled kernels optimized per card or generic shims?
[00:12:08] Maya Chen: We ship both: generic portable kernels and specialized optimized kernels for certain cards. The optimized ones give measurable latency wins but are more fragile across driver versions.
[00:12:20] Ravi Patel: Let's talk numbers — what p95 reductions have you seen with KV prefetch + active warmup?
[00:12:27] Maya Chen: On chat workloads with long contexts we've seen p95 drop from ~700ms to ~220–300ms with a combination of persistent KV and active warmup, plus low-latency lanes enabled. Exact numbers depend on model size and hardware.
[00:12:41] Marco Vega: And batching impact on throughput?
[00:12:45] Jonah Ruiz: Batching typically gives 2.5–5x token throughput uplift depending on beam size and model. For mixed lanes you still preserve low-latency tail.
[00:12:55] Ravi Patel: For the warmup we need sample scripts. Also would like the kernel pack checksums.
[00:13:02] Alec Park: We'll send kernel pack manifests and a warmup script repo.
[00:13:08] [00:13:08] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[00:13:22] Marco Vega: One more ops question — how do we handle rolling restarts without warming back to cold?
[00:13:30] Maya Chen: We suggest draining nodes and migrating active KV snapshots before evicting pods, or using a shared persistent volume with encrypted snapshots. There's also a fast restore API that streams snapshot state into newly created pods to minimize cold windows.
[00:13:49] Priya Singh: For on-site run test — what telemetry should we gather to decide go/no-go?
[00:13:56] Jonah Ruiz: p50/p95 token latencies, batch sizes, KV hit-rate, kernel fallback occurrences, GPU utilization, and memory pressure. We'll share a Prometheus dashboard template.
[00:14:10] Dana Lopez: How intrusive is the perf harness — can we run it during a maintenance window without impacting production?
[00:14:18] Maya Chen: It's designed for maintenance windows; load is synthetic and you can throttle QPS. For safety, run on a subset of nodes.
[00:14:26] Ravi Patel: Ok let's step to next steps.
[00:14:30] Alec Park: Recap actions: I'll send the bundle manifest, license template and kernel pack checksums. Maya will produce a KV-prefetch tuning doc and the warmup scripts. We want your GPU list and any driver whitelist by Aug 12 so we can pre-validate. We'll plan the 2-hour on-site run on Aug 20.
[00:14:51] Marco Vega: Sounds good. Also we'll need an SOW for the on-site support hours.
[00:14:57] Alec Park: We'll attach an SOW draft in Slack.
[00:15:02] [Crosstalk — multiple speakers agreeing]
[00:15:18] Ravi Patel: Thanks everyone. Good call, lots of clear items.
[00:15:24] Alec Park: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of recording.
